title: Predictable AI spend in BigQuery: Introducing cost management for generative AI functions
raw_text:
The generative AI functions in BigQuery ( AI.GENERATE , AI.IF , AI.CLASSIFY , AI.SCORE , and more) bring large language models (LLMs) directly into your SQL, so a single query can classify millions of support tickets or score each product review for sentiment. However, because these functions are billed by the token, scaling them across massive datasets highlights the importance of managing your budget proactively. We recently announced the general availability (GA) of token-based cost management for BigQuery generative AI functions : daily quotas that let administrators set self-serve guardrails on AI token consumption, so teams can innovate while staying within your budget. In this blog, we provide an overview of cost management for BigQuery generative AI functions, walk through a few practical examples, and share resources to help you get started. Let’s jump in. Quotas for managing costs Four daily quotas, managed through the Google Cloud Identity and Access Management (IAM) quota system, provide controls at the project level and the per-user level. Per-user limits apply to each user within a project, not across your organization. Quota name Metric Scope Default value AI input tokens per day Input tokens used by the LLM Per day, per project 200 billion AI input tokens per day per user Input tokens used by the LLM Per day, per project, per user 150 billion AI output tokens per day Output and thinking tokens used by the LLM Per day, per project, per project 20 billion AI output tokens per day per user Output and thinking tokens used by the LLM Per day, per project, per user 15 billion Key details: The quotas are global. Usage is summed across all regions, so costs can't pile up unnoticed in a region you weren't watching. Output quotas include "thinking" tokens. Reasoning tokens count toward your output quota, just as they count toward your Gemini platform bill. Which functions are covered? The quotas apply to these BigQuery functions that perform LLM-backed generation: AI.GENERATE AI.GENERATE_TABLE AI.GENERATE_TEXT (and its alias ML.GENERATE_TEXT ) AI.CLASSIFY AI.IF AI.SCORE AI.AGG What's not covered: Embedding functions such as AI.GENERATE_EMBEDDING (also available as ML.GENERATE_EMBEDDING ) and AI.EMBED are not subject to these quotas, because they run on different, substantially cheaper models. Managing your quotas Administrators can view and adjust the quotas directly in the Google Cloud console as workloads change, with no support case required. Navigate to IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits . Filter by service and select BigQuery API . Sort by the Name column to bring the four AI quotas to the top. Locating the gen AI token quotas in IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits. 4. Find the quota, for example AI input tokens per day . 5. Open the three-dot menu and choose Edit quota . From there: To tighten cost control, lower a quota. This takes effect immediately with no approval needed. To support higher usage, request an increase from the same page. Many requests are auto-approved; larger increases may go through a quick review. Editing a gen AI token quota in IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits. You'll need the right permissions. You need one of: Owner , Editor, Quota Administrator ( roles/servicemanagement.quotaAdmin ), or Service Usage Admin ( roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin ). Prefer automation? You can also manage these quotas programmatically through the Cloud Quotas API , the gcloud CLI, and Terraform to apply consistent guardrails across projects. Monitoring usage Beyond setting limits, the Quotas & System Limits page displays your historical token consumption so you can quickly detect spikes and right-size your budgets. Use these trends to see how new generative AI workloads and data pipelines affect your overall token usage. Daily project-level token usage for a gen AI token quota in IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits. Longer-term usage graph with selectable 7-day, 14-day, 30-day, and custom ranges. For a step-by-step walkthrough, see the BigQuery documentation on controlling costs with token quotas . Token quotas vs. billing spend caps Token quotas aren't the only cost guardrail in Google Cloud. Token quotas (this feature) are preventive and AI-specific . BigQuery tracks token usage during query execution and stops work close to the limit, with separate limits per project and per user. Cloud Billing spend caps operate on dollars at the project and service level and can automatically block usage when a threshold is reached. They're a broad, financial backstop rather than a precise usage control, and because enforcement is not instant, some overages are incurred. Use token quotas as your first line of defense for AI spend, and a spend cap as a project-wide safety net. How enforcement works Quotas are enforced by stopping work rather than letting a query run past your limit. A query is rejected up front with a QuotaExceeded error only if a quota it needs is already exhausted. Otherwise, it starts, and if a quota runs out mid-query, BigQuery stops sending new LLM calls: Functions that support max_error_ratio (such as AI.IF ) return partial results if unprocessed rows stay within the ratio, and otherwise fail. General-purpose functions (such as AI.GENERATE ) still succeed. Skipped rows have no generated value, and their status field contains the quota-exceeded error. For details, see quota enforcement behavior in the documentation. Sizing your input data: AI.COUNT_TOKENS To choose quota values, it helps to know how much text your workloads send to a model. The AI.COUNT_TOKENS function helps with this. AI.COUNT_TOKENS returns the number of tokens a model's tokenizer produces for a text string, without making a billable generation call. Run it over a column to measure your input data: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Count the input text tokens for each product review
SELECT
 SUM(
 AI.COUNT_TOKENS(
 CONCAT('Classify the sentiment of this review as positive, negative, or neutral: ', review_text),

 endpoint => 'gemini-3.1-flash-lite').result) AS total_input_tokens
FROM
 `my_project.my_dataset.product_reviews`;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbb67880910>)])]> The count is a lower bound on input tokens. It doesn't include output or thinking tokens, the instructions each AI function adds around your input, or non-text inputs such as images. Use it to: Gauge the input side of a workload before you launch it. Right-size your quotas together with a small sample run that measures actual input and output usage. Translate tokens into dollars using the published Gemini platform pricing for your model. From tokens to budget: a worked example Suppose you want to keep a project's daily AI spend around $100 with the Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite model. As of today's published pricing (BigQuery processes in batch which provides a 50% discount): Input tokens: $0.125 per 1 million tokens Output tokens (response + reasoning): $0.75 per 1 million tokens If a small sample run shows an average 100:1 input-to-output token ratio , you can solve for a daily budget: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Cost: 0.125 × I + 0.75 × O = 100 (I, O in millions of tokens)
Ratio: I = 100 × O'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbb67e6e6d0>)])]> Solving gives about 754 million input tokens and 7.54 million output tokens per day. Set AI input tokens per day and AI output tokens per day to these values to hold the project near $100/day. If a project uses models with different prices, budget per model or blend the rates. Best practices for managing AI cost Start with per-user quotas. They stop one user or runaway experiment from draining the project's budget. Measure before you scale. Use AI.COUNT_TOKENS to size your input, then check a small sample run in the usage chart before setting limits. Mind the output side. Output tokens cost more. Where a function accepts max_output_tokens , set it to bound generation length. Monitor and iterate. Adjust limits as real usage and budgets change. Get started Token-based cost management is available now. To begin: Open IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits in the Google Cloud Console and filter by BigQuery API . Review the four AI-related token quotas and set limits that match your budget. Use AI.COUNT_TOKENS to size your input data. For the full details, see the documentation on controlling generative AI costs . With token-based guardrails in place, your teams can use generative AI in BigQuery with the cost predictability your organization needs.

Today, Stephanie Kiel explains the latest on our approach to post-quantum cryptography, and shares a new tool to help CISOs and executives prepare their organizations for PQC. As with all Cloud CISO Perspectives, the contents of this newsletter are posted to the Google Cloud blog . If you’re reading this on the website and you’d like to receive the email version, you can subscribe here . aside_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('title', 'Get vital board insights with Google Cloud'), ('body', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbb66c3b150>), ('btn_text', 'Visit the hub'), ('href', 'https://cloud.google.com/solutions/security/board-of-directors?utm_source=cgc-site&utm_medium=et&utm_campaign=FY26-Q2-GLOBAL-GCP39634-email-dl-dgcsm-CISOP-NL-177159&utm_content=-&utm_term=-'), ('image', <GAEImage: GCAT-replacement-logo-A>)])]> New Gemini Notebook can help CISOs and policymakers prepare for PQC By Stephanie Kiel, Head of Cloud Security Policy, Government Affairs and Public Policy, Google Cloud Stephanie Kiel, Head of Cloud Security Policy, Government Affairs and Public Policy, Google Cloud Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is one of the most urgent security shifts of the decade — and one of the easiest to tune out. For security leaders and policymakers, the research is dense, scattered across papers and engineering blogs, and can be challenging to turn into action. To help, we're launching Prepare for Post-Quantum Cryptography , a public Gemini Notebook that brings Google's PQC research, engineering blogs, and migration guidance together in one place. Ask it questions, listen to an audio overview, or test yourself with flashcards, and quickly get up to speed on the quantum threat. Why PQC matters now Quantum computing is rapidly moving from theory to reality. Our Willow chip and Quantum Echoes algorithm mark substantial progress, and Google research estimates that breaking ECDLP-256 and RSA-2048 encryption — the public-key cryptography schemes protecting much of our online data — would require around 500,000 and 1 million imperfect quantum computer components (noisy qubits), respectively. To help, we're launching Prepare for Post-Quantum Cryptography, a public Gemini Notebook that brings Google's PQC research, engineering blogs, and migration guidance together in one place. This research has consequences now. It indicates that today’s online security is more vulnerable to future quantum computers than previously thought. In Store Now, Decrypt Later attacks, adversaries may steal encrypted data now and wait to decrypt it once a sufficiently powerful quantum computer exists. Data that we’ve long considered sensitive — health records, financial data, intellectual property, and government secrets — is already at risk . With continued advances in architecture, quantum algorithms, and quantum error correction shrinking future quantum hardware requirements, waiting to upgrade our digital locks is not a viable option. To help organizations stay ahead of the curve, Google has published a migration timeline noting our plans to transition to PQC by 2029, and we urge others to consider the same. As the technology advances, policymakers should consider urging critical infrastructure owners and operators to recognize condensed timelines, and build PQC readiness into existing risk mitigation plans. We also recommend governments engage with global counterparts to promote a harmonized approach to standards development, and include technical and security experts in the building of policy and regulatory requirements focused on quantum safety. Google's PQC expertise, in one notebook The Prepare for Post-Quantum Cryptography notebook turns years of Google expertise into an interactive primer that anyone can use. It's built on curated Google sources covering the quantum era, quantum computing breakthroughs like Willow, Quantum Echoes, and surface code error suppression, industry PQC standards, Google's own deployments, and the latest research. In the Gemini Notebook, you can: Get answers grounded in Google's sources. Listen to a podcast-style audio overview. Test your PQC knowledge with flashcards. Explore an interactive visual diagram of the quantum threat. Read a concise briefing document. Try these prompts To get started, here are a few questions to ask the notebook: For CISOs : "What should a CISO prioritize in the first 90 days of a PQC migration?" For anyone new to PQC : "Explain store-now-decrypt-later in plain terms." For developers : "How does hybrid ML-KEM key exchange work in Chrome?" As with all generative AI, the notebook can make mistakes, so check its responses against the linked sources. What's at stake Previous cryptographic migrations, such as moving from SHA-1 or upgrading TLS, have taken a decade or more. Waiting for the availability of a cryptographically-relevant quantum computer before beginning the migration journey represents a significant security risk given the importance of public-key cryptography for securing digital essentials like web traffic, software updates, digital identities, and signatures. For CISOs, we recommend that you start by: Understanding where vulnerable cryptography lives in your organization. Identifying and prioritizing data and systems most at risk from quantum threats, and developing a plan for addressing these risks. Anticipate system-wide effects that PQC migration could have. Building crypto-agility into your security plans, using learnings from past experiences like Heartbleed. Additional detail on these recommendations is available in our previous blog post . For the broader security community, the transition only succeeds if this knowledge is accessible to everyone — not just organizations with dedicated cryptography teams. How Google is putting PQC into practice We’ve been deploying PQC for years. Highlights include: Hybrid Kyber/ML-KEM key exchange protecting Chrome traffic PQC in Android Quantum-safe digital signatures in Cloud KMS PQC for Google's internal communications Wiz PQC readiness scanner across code, cloud, and runtime We also co-founded the Post-Quantum Cryptography Alliance at the Linux Foundation with industry leaders including Amazon Web Services, Cisco, IBM, and NVIDIA to support open-source tools like Open Quantum Safe . Have experts check every artifact before you share it. Start preparing today The quantum transition has already started, but preparing your organization doesn't have to begin with a 100-page whitepaper. Start by understanding the threat, then assess your cryptographic inventory and build a migration roadmap. title: Cross-cloud conversational analytics made simple with open standards
raw_text:
The reality for most organizations is that data lives everywhere. As engineering teams expand and adopt specialized platforms for their workloads, enterprise data naturally disperses across multiple clouds and operational systems. When analytical and AI initiatives require context from across the entire organization,these teams traditionally face a difficult trade-off: build complex extraction pipelines to copy data into a central repository or accept fragmented reporting. Traditional architectures address this fragmentation with scheduled extraction pipelines that copy remote datasets into a central staging warehouse. This approach creates synchronization lag, adds recurring storage costs, and triggers variable network egress fees. When schemas change upstream, pipelines break, and teams spend hours reconciling metrics across out-of-sync dashboards. BigQuery and Google Cloud’s borderless Lakehouse offer a streamlined way to solve this challenge with a foundation based on the open Apache Iceberg REST catalog specification. Rather than moving data to the compute engine, you can bring Google Cloud compute and generative AI directly to your data, querying it in place across Databricks, Snowflake, and AWS Glue. In this post, we walk through how to configure Databricks Unity Catalog for federation into BigQuery (AWS Glue and Snowflake set up in appendix), run a single query joining data across all three external catalogs, and use conversational analytics in BigQuery to explore the consolidated data with natural language. Figure 1: BigQuery federates metadata across external Apache Iceberg REST catalogs through Lakehouse, enabling in-place conversational analytics without data migration. The borderless lakehouse architecture This solution uses Lakehouse runtime catalog to synchronize metadata from other cloud providers, allowing you to query data with BigQuery or external open source engines through the Apache Iceberg REST catalog endpoint, all without migrating the data. Because Databricks Unity Catalog, Snowflake Horizon Catalog, and AWS Glue Data Catalog support the open Apache Iceberg REST catalog specification, you can apply a consistent connection pattern across all three platforms. When you run a federated query, Lakehouse runtime catalog separates metadata synchronization from storage access: Metadata synchronization: Lakehouse runtime catalog periodically syncs schemas, snapshot pointers, and table definitions from the remote catalog based on a refresh schedule you define. Direct storage access: During query runtime, a compatible engine reads Parquet data files directly from remote object storage, such as Amazon S3, using temporary credentials issued by the remote platform. All query processing runs within Google cloud compute such as BigQuery or Managed Service for Apache Spark . Remote Databricks clusters, Snowflake virtual warehouses, and AWS compute instances are not invoked during execution. Authentication follows an explicit three-step deployment pattern: create the federated catalog in Google Cloud, inspect its configuration to retrieve its automatically generated service account, and grant access permissions within the remote platform. You can use AI to generate sample data. The schema details for tables are provided below. Configure Databricks Unity Catalog We begin in Databricks by preparing the catalog and table. In Unity Catalog, federated access requires that your target schema be associated with an external location registered in Databricks: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Run inside Databricks SQL workspace
CREATE CATALOG IF NOT EXISTS dbx_retail_db;

-- Declare the managed target location at the schema level
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS dbx_retail_db.dbx_core 
 MANAGED LOCATION 's3://my-databricks-bucket/retail/data/';

-- Create the Iceberg dimension table
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS dbx_retail_db.dbx_core.dim_products (
 product_key INT,
 product_id STRING,
 product_name STRING,
 category STRING,
 subcategory STRING,
 brand STRING,
 price DOUBLE,
 cost DOUBLE
)
USING iceberg;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbb6759fbd0>)])]> You can use AI to generate sample data. The schema details for tables are provided in each section. Before external engines can read this table, a Databricks metastore administrator must enable External data access on the metastore details tab. Go to Databricks Admin account and under User Management, create a Databricks Service Principal and make a note of its UUID "6ea7b861-c5a5-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx" Connect Databricks to BigQuery Next, create the federated catalog inside Google Cloud using the gcloud command-line tool. You will need your Databricks workspace URL and the application ID of your Databricks service principal: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'export GCP_PROJECT_ID="my-lakehouse-project"
export GCP_REGION="us-central1"

gcloud alpha biglake iceberg catalogs create dbx_retail_db \
 --project="$GCP_PROJECT_ID" \
 --primary-location="$GCP_REGION" \
 --catalog-type="federated" \
 --federated-catalog-type="unity" \
 --unity-instance-name="dbc-xxxxxxxx-xxxx.cloud.databricks.com" \
 --unity-catalog-name="dbx_retail_db" \
 --unity-service-principal-application-id="6ea7b861-c5a5-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx" \
 --refresh-interval="300s"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbb66c12290>)])]> Once created, describe the catalog to view its assigned service account: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud alpha biglake iceberg catalogs describe dbx_retail_db \
 --project="$GCP_PROJECT_ID"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbb66cb0150>)])]> Return to Databricks to assign permissions to your service principal: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '-- Grant catalog traversal permission
GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG dbx_retail_db 
 TO `6ea7b861-c5a5-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx`;

-- Grant schema and read permissions
GRANT USE SCHEMA,EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA, SELECT ON SCHEMA dbx_retail_db.dbx_core 
 TO `6ea7b861-c5a5-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx`;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbb66cb00d0>)])]> You must grant the EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA privilege to the Databricks Service Principal on the target schemas or catalog to enable credential vending for external data access. Finally, to complete the connection, configure the federation policy on the Databricks service principal with the following details - Issuer URL* - https://accounts.google.com Subject* - numeric subject ID returned by the catalog describe command eg 1124251400450xxxxxxxx Audiences - https://accounts.cloud.databricks.com Run one query across three clouds Federated Iceberg tables are addressed in BigQuery using four-part paths: project.catalog.namespace.table . In our environment, sales transactions reside natively in BigQuery: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS local_retail_dataset
OPTIONS(location="us-central1");

CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE `my-lakehouse-project.local_retail_dataset.fact_sales` (
 sale_id STRING,
 sale_date DATE,
 customer_key INT64,
 product_key INT64,
 store_key INT64,
 quantity INT64,
 unit_price NUMERIC,
 discount NUMERIC,
 total_revenue NUMERIC,
 total_cost NUMERIC,
 margin NUMERIC
)
PARTITION BY sale_date
CLUSTER BY store_key, product_key;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbb66cb2090>)])]> We can now run a single SQL query joining our native sales transactions with customer records in Snowflake, product lines in Databricks, and store locations in AWS Glue: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "SELECT 
 c.first_name || ' ' || c.last_name AS customer_name, -- From Snowflake Iceberg
 p.product_name, -- From Databricks Iceberg
 s.store_name, -- From AWS S3 Iceberg
 SUM(f.quantity) AS total_units_sold, -- From BigQuery native fact
 SUM(f.total_revenue) AS total_sales_revenue -- From BigQuery native fact
FROM `my-lakehouse-project.local_retail_dataset.fact_sales` f
INNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.sf_retail_db.CORE.DIM_CUSTOMERS` c 
 ON f.customer_key = c.customer_key
INNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.dbx_retail_db.dbx_core.dim_products` p 
 ON f.product_key = p.product_key
INNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.glue_retail_db.glue_retail_db.dim_stores` s 
 ON f.store_key = s.store_key
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
ORDER BY total_sales_revenue DESC
LIMIT 10;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbb67006c50>)])]> BigQuery processes the joins in place. Notice that Snowflake identifiers appear in uppercase ( CORE.DIM_CUSTOMERS ), while Databricks and AWS Glue maintain lowercase table paths. Figure 2 - Query results combining data across Snowflake, Databricks, and AWS Glue. Explore cross-cloud data with natural language Because federated Iceberg tables behave like native tables within BigQuery, downstream analytical features inherit access directly. You can point conversational analytics in BigQuery at these federated schemas to let team members explore cross-cloud data using natural language prompts. To give conversational analytics full operational context, we save our federated join as a logical view: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW `my-lakehouse-project.local_retail_dataset.v_omnichannel_sales_pulse` AS
SELECT 
 f.sale_id,
 f.sale_date,
 c.first_name || ' ' || c.last_name AS customer_name,
 c.country AS customer_country,
 p.product_name,
 p.category AS product_category,
 p.brand AS product_brand,
 s.store_name,
 s.city AS store_city,
 s.region AS store_region,
 f.quantity,
 f.total_revenue,
 f.margin
FROM `my-lakehouse-project.local_retail_dataset.fact_sales` f
INNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.sf_retail_db.CORE.DIM_CUSTOMERS` c 
 ON f.customer_key = c.customer_key
INNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.dbx_retail_db.dbx_core.dim_products` p 
 ON f.product_key = p.product_key
INNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.glue_retail_db.glue_retail_db.dim_stores` s 
 ON f.store_key = s.store_key;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbb67eab250>)])]> Analyze sales performance in natural language When you ask conversational analytics in BigQuery: "Who are our top customers by total sales revenue, what products did they buy, and which stores did they shop at?" Conversational analytics evaluates the schema across all three remote catalogs, generates the SQL statement, executes the query, and presents the response. Figure 3: Conversational analytics in BigQuery translates plain-language prompts into federated queries across Snowflake, Databricks, and AWS Glue. Plan for caching and data residency Before deploying federated catalogs in production, consider these operational behaviors: Background refresh timing: The --refresh-interval flag controls metadata synchronization. The minimum interval is 300 seconds. For larger catalogs containing hundreds of tables, metadata retrieval can take longer. If a sync cycle overruns, BigQuery skips the next scheduled run to avoid task queuing. Automatic query caching: BigQuery caches retrieved cross-cloud data blocks in the region where your federated catalog resides (e.g. us-central1 ). This helps reduce network transfer on repeated queries. Because cached blocks reside within Google Cloud storage in that region, confirm that this aligns with your organization's data residency policies. Encryption controls: Cross-cloud cache blocks use Google-managed encryption keys. If your organization enforces the constraints/gcp.restrictNonCmekServices policy constraint, BigQuery bypasses the cache and reads directly from remote storage for every query. Monitoring access metrics: You can evaluate cache utilization in your query execution plans. Check the objectStorageStats section in BigQuery job statistics to compare cacheBytesRead against objectStorageBytesRead . Next steps In summary, Google Cloud’s borderless Lakehouse helps you activate your data regardless of where it lives without costly migrations or building additional data pipelines. Get started today by reviewing the borderless Lakehouse architecture documentation to learn more about supported regions and credential configurations. You can work through the borderless Lakehouse codelab to practice federating external catalogs step-by-step. Finally, connect with your Google Cloud account team or customer engineer to evaluate borderless lakehouse patterns for your specific data platforms or industries. Appendix Setting up Snowflake and AWS Glue cross cloud data access Connect Snowflake and Big Query Configure Snowflake Horizon Catalog We begin in Snowflake by creating the database, schema, and Iceberg table. In Snowflake Horizon, managed Iceberg tables expose an open Apache Iceberg REST catalog interface automatically: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Run inside Snowflake SQL worksheet
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS sf_retail_db;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS sf_retail_db.core;

-- Create the Iceberg dimension table
CREATE OR REPLACE ICEBERG TABLE sf_retail_db.core.dim_customers (
 customer_key INTEGER,
 customer_id VARCHAR,
 first_name VARCHAR,
 last_name VARCHAR,
 email VARCHAR,
 gender VARCHAR,
 country VARCHAR,
 signup_date DATE

)
CATALOG = 'SNOWFLAKE'
EXTERNAL_VOLUME = 'SNOWFLAKE_MANAGED';"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbb67ea9390>)])]> Before external engines can read this catalog, configure a dedicated reader role and grant traversal permissions across the database, schema, and table. SQL code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '-- Create a dedicated reader role
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS gcp_lakehouse_reader_role;

-- Grant database and schema traversal permissions
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE sf_retail_db TO ROLE gcp_lakehouse_reader_role;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA sf_retail_db.core TO ROLE gcp_lakehouse_reader_role;

-- Grant read access on the target table
GRANT SELECT ON TABLE sf_retail_db.core.dim_customers TO ROLE gcp_lakehouse_reader_role;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbb67b5b750>)])]> Next, create the federated catalog inside Google Cloud using the gcloud command-line tool. You will need your Snowflake account identifier, the reader role, and the root Iceberg database name: bash code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'export GCP_PROJECT_ID="my-lakehouse-project"
export GCP_REGION="us-central1"

gcloud alpha biglake iceberg catalogs create sf_retail_db \
 --project="$GCP_PROJECT_ID" \
 --primary-location="$GCP_REGION" \
 --catalog-type="federated" \
 --federated-catalog-type="snowflake" \
 --snowflake-account-identifier="xy12345-ab67890" \
 --snowflake-warehouse="SF_RETAIL_DB" \
 --snowflake-role="gcp_lakehouse_reader_role" \
 --refresh-interval="300s"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbb75773a50>)])]> In the Apache Iceberg REST specification, --snowflake-warehouse references the catalog root database name ( SF_RETAIL_DB ), not a virtual compute warehouse. Once created, describe the catalog to view its assigned numeric service account ID: bash code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud alpha biglake iceberg catalogs describe sf_retail_db \
 --project="$GCP_PROJECT_ID" \
 --format='value(biglake-service-account-id)''), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbb67237d10>)])]> Return to Snowflake to bind Google Cloud's numeric identity to a passwordless service user via Workload Identity Federation (WIF): SQL code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Run inside Snowflake SQL worksheet
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;

-- Bind Google Cloud's numeric identity to a passwordless service user
CREATE OR REPLACE USER snowflake_service_user
 TYPE = SERVICE
 WORKLOAD_IDENTITY = (
 TYPE = GCP
 SUBJECT = '102669xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx' -- Numeric subject ID returned by gcloud describe
 )
 DEFAULT_ROLE = gcp_lakehouse_reader_role
 COMMENT = 'Service user for Lakehouse catalog federation over WIF';

-- Grant the reader role to this service user
GRANT ROLE gcp_lakehouse_reader_role TO USER snowflake_service_user;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbb67237e90>)])]> This establishes passwordless authentication over OpenID Connect, allowing BigQuery to discover table metadata and vend temporary query-time credentials directly from Snowflake Horizon. Configure AWS Glue Data Catalog We begin in AWS by preparing the IAM identity, establishing access permissions across AWS Glue and Amazon S3, and registering the Iceberg table. First, create a placeholder trust policy named trust_policy.json . This allows you to provision the AWS IAM role before Google Cloud assigns the unique catalog service agent: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '{
 "Version": "2012-10-17",
 "Statement": [
 {
 "Effect": "Allow",
 "Principal": {
 "Federated": "accounts.google.com"
 },
 "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
 "Condition": {
 "StringEquals": {
 "accounts.google.com:aud": ["PLACEHOLDER_VALUE"],
 "accounts.google.com:sub": ["PLACEHOLDER_VALUE"]
 }
 }
 }
 ]
}'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbb67123050>)])]> Create the IAM role using the AWS CLI. Setting a 12-hour session duration ( 43200 seconds) prevents credential expiration during long-running analytical queries: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'export AWS_ROLE_NAME="lakehouse_glue_federation_role"

aws iam create-role \
 --role-name "$AWS_ROLE_NAME" \
 --assume-role-policy-document file://trust_policy.json \
 --max-session-duration 43200'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbb671234d0>)])]> Next, define the permissions policy in a file named permissions_policy.json . This policy grants BigQuery permission to read the AWS Glue catalog metadata and access the underlying Parquet data files in Amazon S3: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '{
 "Version": "2012-10-17",
 "Statement": [
 {
 "Sid": "GlueCatalogRead",
 "Effect": "Allow",
 "Action": [
 "glue:GetCatalog",
 "glue:GetDatabase",
 "glue:GetDatabases",
 "glue:GetTable",
 "glue:GetTables"
 ],
 "Resource": "arn:aws:glue:us-east-2:123456789012:*"
 },
 {
 "Sid": "S3BucketAndObjectRead",
 "Effect": "Allow",
 "Action": [
 "s3:ListBucket",
 "s3:GetObject"
 ],
 "Resource": [
 "arn:aws:s3:::my-glue-iceberg-bucket",
 "arn:aws:s3:::my-glue-iceberg-bucket/*"
 ]
 }
 ]
}'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbb67121bd0>)])]> Attach this permissions policy to your newly created role: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'aws iam put-role-policy \
 --role-name "$AWS_ROLE_NAME" \
 --policy-name "lakehouse_glue_federation_policy" \
 --policy-document file://permissions_policy.json'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbb67120e10>)])]> Important (AWS Lake Formation): If your AWS environment uses AWS Lake Formation, verify that the IAMAllowedPrincipals group has access to the target database and table (or grant explicit Lake Formation permissions to lakehouse_glue_federation_role if the bucket is registered with AWS Lake Formation ). Without this, Lake Formation security settings will block the IAM role from accessing catalog metadata. With permissions in place, create the database and Iceberg table in AWS Glue using Amazon Athena: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Run inside Amazon Athena
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS glue_retail_db;

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS glue_retail_db.dim_stores (
 store_key INT,
 store_id STRING,
 store_name STRING,
 city STRING,
 state STRING,
 region STRING,
 manager STRING,
 opened_date DATE

)
LOCATION 's3://my-glue-iceberg-bucket/retail/dim_stores/'
TBLPROPERTIES (
 'table_type'='ICEBERG', 
 'format'='parquet', 
 'write_compression'='zstd' 

);"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbb672dae10>)])]> Connect AWS Glue to BigQuery Next, register the federated catalog inside Google Cloud using the gcloud command-line tool. You will need your 12-digit AWS Account ID, AWS Region, and the role ARN created above: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'export GCP_PROJECT_ID="my-lakehouse-project"
export GCP_REGION="us-central1"
export AWS_REGION="us-east-2"
export AWS_ACCOUNT_ID="123456789012"

gcloud alpha biglake iceberg catalogs create glue_retail_db \
 --project="$GCP_PROJECT_ID" \
 --primary-location="$GCP_REGION" \
 --catalog-type="federated" \

title: As phishing-as-a-service goes industrial, Microsoft takes down a marketplace behind 1 billion messages
raw_text: Microsoft says it has dismantled a criminal marketplace responsible for 1 billion malicious messages. Working with international authorities and several tech and cybersecurity companies in a nearly year-long investigation, Redmond identified and took down Yam Store, a coordinated underground network dealing in commercial phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS). The network allowed cybercriminals to readily purchase, and very quickly deploy, pre-made kits they could use in phishing attacks to steal data and credentials. Microsoft said the takedown began as a simple investigation based on a tip from Japanese authorities. “Working together, and with the assistance of AI tools, we connected accounts, websites, and infrastructure that initially appeared unrelated, helping expose the broader criminal marketplace behind them,” Steven Masada , associate general counsel and GM for Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit, wrote in a blog post . “What appears to be a simple scam message is often the visible end of a much larger transnational cybercriminal operation.” The evolving PhaaS marketplace Collectively, YAM Store and the kits and tools sold within it enabled the sending of more than 1 billion messages to 75,000-plus organizations worldwide. More than 750 million of those were sent to Microsoft customers alone, and ultimately generated “tens of millions of dollars” for criminal operators. Investigation into the marketplace began in late 2025 after Japan’s National Police Agency (NPA) notified Microsoft of “a wave of fraud and scam activity” targeting people and businesses in Japan. Researchers expected to find multiple individual campaigns; instead, they discovered a “sprawling Chinese-language cybercrime marketplace.” The probe expanded globally and involved the efforts of several other law enforcement agencies, as well as companies like Resecurity, Cloudflare, Oracle, Proofpoint, and TRM Labs. The YAM Store served as an initial access broker (IAB), operating much like an online marketplace; in this case, the merchandise was fraudulent Microsoft and Google accounts and other ready-made tools used to carry out scams like credential and data theft. Customers could browse, compare prices, and make purchases. Available tools were arranged based on age and subscription and environment types (like .edu or .org sites). In some cases, criminal operators were able to register internet domains that legitimate organizations had allowed to expire, then rebuilt them to appear active. They targeted specific sectors (like non-profits or education) to fraudulently obtain Microsoft 365 accounts to later sell through the YAM store. The researchers discovered that the YAM Store evolved as different kits became available, and identified three popular PhaaS kits: Iron Man System, CoGUI, and Haozi. The newer Iron Man system came to the fore in mid-2026. It provided pre-built lure pages capturing any victim-submitted data. The lure sites impersonated healthcare providers, police departments, government agencies, postal and courier services, toll and transportation authorities, tax agencies, banks, telecoms, and retailers. Through test purchases and intelligence work, investigators discovered more than 2,300 templates impersonating organizations across more than 150 countries. Iron Man effectively expanded the PhaaS model by giving criminals access to thousands of ready-made templates tailored to specific industries, languages, and regions. Masada noted that many “used the appearance of official authority to pressure victims into making payments or disclosing sensitive personal information. Instead of creating fraudulent websites themselves, criminals could quickly deploy pages designed to steal passwords, payment information, and other personal data.” The kits were also equipped with advanced evasion techniques such as geofencing, fake CAPTCHA gates, IP address blocklists and allowlists, and anti-detection configurations. Masada emphasized that, while an organization or government entity may have been presented among the template offerings, it does not indicate that its systems were compromised. However, members of the Microsoft Threat Intelligence and Microsoft Digital Crimes Unit wrote in a blog post , “the scale and proliferation of this ecosystem demonstrate how readily available criminal infrastructure can lower the barrier to entry, enabling less skilled cybercriminals to target organizations at scale and contribute to fraud losses.” The importance of cyber hygiene In nearly all observed cases, phishing lures presented “prescriptive scam red flags,” Microsoft researchers explained: Urgency and time-sensitive tasks. They advised that users have a basic understanding of common phishing techniques and should be educated to always verify with the purported sender before clicking a link supposedly taking them to a login page, even when the task involves signing in to a known, secure account. Beyond this, they said, sign-in prompts should clearly identify the application being authenticated to. In Microsoft Azure interactions since 2021, for example, users are prompted to “cancel” or “continue” at login, but this is often missing from phishing sign-ins, the researchers noted. Hardening credentials and cloud identities is also necessary to defend against phishing attacks; the researchers suggested an initial step of passwordless tools like passkeys and multifactor authentication (MFA) across organizations. “Invoke the principles of least privilege and zero trust to significantly slow down threat actors who might have been able to gain initial access and buy time for defenders to respond,” the researchers noted. These steps can help lock down global administrator roles in particular. They also advised additional actions including the use of the Microsoft Authenticator app for passkeys and MFA; configuration of the Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Safe Links policy to apply to internal recipients; complementing MFA with conditional access policies; and only allowing MFA and passkey registrations from trusted locations and devices.

title: How Claude Code’s 256KB blind spot put developers’ secrets in the preview pane
raw_text: Simply asking Anthropic’s Claude Code to review an HTML file could hand attackers access to a developer’s machine, cloud credentials and software development environment, according to a new Noma Security finding. Noma’s researchers found a vulnerability affecting Anthropic’s Claude Code Desktop app that could allow malicious JavaScript embedded in an HTML file to execute without further user interaction, potentially exposing sensitive host files. The flaw, called SneakPeek, specifically affected the application’s automated preview pane, which renders HTML files generated or modified by Claude. “This is a strong example of how emerging technologies are reshaping the attack surface,” said Ronald Lewis , head of cybersecurity governance at Black Duck. “Attackers are increasingly targeting the AI ecosystem, exploiting implicit trust relationships between models, agents, tools, data sources, and connected services.” An attacker could exploit the bug by planting a malicious file in a public repository and waiting for a developer to ask Claude Code to inspect it, Noma said in a blog post shared with CSO ahead of its publication on Wednesday. Once the application rendered the file, the script could read local files and exfiltrate sensitive data, including AWS credentials , GitHub secrets and SSH private keys, to a remote server. The flaw has been assigned a high-severity CVSS score of 8.7, while a CVE ID is not yet available. Noma says Anthropic collaborated with Noma Labs during the disclosure process and fully resolved the issue. “Anthropic confirmed they are preparing a GitHub Security Advisory and have requested a CVE for it,” Eli Ainhorn , senior AI vulnerability researcher at Noma, told CSO. “We expect it to be available soon. The CVSS score is 8.7 High (v4.0), assigned by Anthropic. Anthropic did not immediately respond to CSO’s request for comment. A 256KB threshold allowed local files to leak Noma traced SneakPeek to three architectural gaps in Claude Code Desktop’s preview mechanism, which uses an Electron-based Chromium rendering panel to display HTML content. The first involved a file-size threshold that changed how the application handled HTML documents. Files smaller than 256KB were converted into base64-encoded data: URLs with a strict Content Security Policy (CSP) that blocked script execution. Files exceeding that threshold were instead written to disk and loaded directly as “file://” URLs, bypassing the CSP protections applied to smaller files. The second problem was the origin assigned to the rendered content. Loading the larger files through file:// gave the preview renderer access to the local filesystem in Chromium rather than confining it to an isolated, opaque origin, the researchers said. The third weakness was an inactive request filter. Although the application has a mechanism intended to block file: // access, Noma found that the filter was not active during static file rendering, including when developers reviewed local code test reports. “Relying on size-based thresholds or client-side filters for security boundaries is inherently fragile,” Lewis said. “Development machines hold high-value operational secrets—SSH private keys, AWS credentials, Kubernetes configurations, and OAuth session tokens.” Compromising a developer’s local workstation is effectively a direct route into corporate cloud infrastructure, he warned. Noma found that Anthropic’s initial patch could be bypassed. “The initial patch blocked the preview pane from making direct file read requests from the main page context, but we found that by moving the file-reading code into a Web Worker, a background thread that browsers run separately from the main page, the requests originated from a context the patch didn’t cover,” Ainhorn explained. The researchers reported the bypass, prompting a deeper architectural fix before the vulnerability was fully resolved. Risk beyond the AI model The malicious script ran inside the preview pane’s rendering process, rather than as an action performed by the AI agent itself. That defeats the assumption that security controls meant for the model are protecting all AI workflows. “The protections were real, they just didn’t cover every path,” Ainhorn said. “Organizations need to keep AI coding tools updated, stop leaving long-lived credentials on developer machines, and use scoped, short-lived tokens where possible. That alone would have limited what this exploit could grab.” According to Sysdig’s senior cybersecurity strategist Crystal Morin , agent-level logs would not necessarily capture the execution. File reads and outbound network connections would instead be visible at the runtime layer, where defenders need appropriate monitoring, Morin said. “The endpoint is where AI agents start, but their blast radius extends to the cloud,“ she added, warning that routine work with AI tools can expose credentials with consequences far beyond the workstation.

title: Hackers abuse the Ivanti Connect Secure bug to gain access without accounts
raw_text: Attackers without an account of their own were found logging in to Ivanti Connect Secure appliances using an authentication bypass flaw that the vendor has since fixed. Once inside, attackers ran arbitrary commands on the appliances. “Ivanti initially discovered a portion of this vulnerability as part of our product security program and patched it in the July release 25.1.3.0,“ the vendor said in a security advisory . ”We had been working to backport the fix to the remaining supported versions when exploitation occurred.” According to security firm watchTowr’s vulnerability FAQ , the flaw allowed remote attackers to spoof the signals used to establish a user’s identity, bypassing normal authentication checks. The bypass uses a path separate from normal authentication, so existing login protections do not stop it, watchTowr added. Tracked as CVE-2026-104935 and rated at CVSS 8.6 out of 10, the vulnerability affects multiple product branches, including Ivanti Connect Secure 22.8R2.4 and earlier, as well as specified 25.1 releases. Ivanti says versions 22.7 and earlier are not affected. Ivanti has released fixes, including for versions 22.8R2.5, 25.1.1.2, 25.1.3.0, and 25.1.3.1, depending on the hardware and software branch. Security teams were advised to identify their deployed versions, apply corresponding fixes, and investigate potential compromise. While Ivanti said reliable indicators of compromise were not yet available, Volexity, the cybersecurity firm credited with discovering the flaw, has published details of its exploitation. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added the flaw to its known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on October 13.

title: Unplug your smart fridges, French supermarkets warned after cyberattack
raw_text: More internet-connected refrigerators have joined the official list of those affected by a cyberattack that ruined stocks of chilled food at hundreds of French supermarkets over the weekend. The French Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-FR) advised supermarkets to disconnect any refrigeration control systems with a public IP address from the internet , and to reconnect them via a secure VPN only after verifying the configuration and, if necessary, restoring factory defaults. In an emergency, it suggested, they could simply filter connections to allow only the IP addresses of their refrigeration suppliers or service providers to connect, but this should not be a long-term solution, CERT-FR said. CERT-FR’s initial warning on Monday listed only Danfoss AK-SC and AK-SM series refrigeration controllers as affected, advising supermarkets to update the firmware of their systems, set the security level to “strict,” and ensure that default passwords had been changed. One of the supermarket chains hardest hit in the attack was Groupement Mousquetaires, which operates under the Intermarché and Netto brands. It promptly removed products from affected fresh and frozen food display units managed by Danfoss in some of its stores, a spokesman said. Following the attack, French control systems vendor Dixell posted presciently on LinkedIn : “Cybersecurity is everyone’s business, all the time. Today, our competitors were targeted; tomorrow, it could be our turn.” And so it came to be. As the list of victims grew, it became apparent that not all the affected supermarkets were using refrigeration controllers supplied by Danfoss, prompting CERT-FR to add other models to the list sold under the Dixell and Copeland brands. Dixell published a security advisory for user of its XWEB internet interface, broadly along the same lines as CERT-FR’s advice. It recommended immediately upgrading systems running version 1.12.1 or older; changing weak or default passwords and activating password security policies on compatible systems; and securing remote access through a VPN, a dedicated 4G mobile data connection, or in an emergency by applying an IP address filter. Tom Hegel, research lead at cybersecurity monitoring company SentinelOne, said the attacks are unlikely to stop with Danfoss and Dixell/Copeland: “With thousands of these interfaces still onine, I expect more incidents like this.” Those interfaces are online because supermarkets often buy “refrigeration as a service,” with providers guaranteeing performance as long as they have access to a constant stream of data from the refrigerators they maintain. The data also enables them to guarantee traceability of the cold chain. As with much legacy operational technology (OT), the security of such systems has largely escaped the notice of CISOs until now. “Retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels, and point-of-sale gear, much of it installed by facilities contractors who rarely loop in the security team,” said Hegel. As they scan and secure their systems, supermarket CISOs will be wondering who attacked them, and why — but with the off switch for their refrigerators effectively posted to the public internet, those will be hard questions to answer. “An attacker who logs into an exposed control panel leaves almost nothing behind, with no malware to analyze and few clues beyond an IP address that probably leads to a rented server. A teenager and an intelligence service would look much the same from the defender’s side,” said Hegel. “The gap between a nuisance and a serious incident often comes down to how much control a victim has exposed to the internet.

title: Cybersecurity is a leadership problem: Why the management model needs to catch up
raw_text: When I started writing regularly about cybersecurity management in 2015 , the environment looked very different. Cloud computing was still reshaping enterprise technology. Ransomware had not become the industrialised threat it is today. Artificial intelligence was not driving boardroom discussions. Zero Trust had yet to enter mainstream technical vocabulary and quantum computing barely registered on the corporate risk horizon. Cybersecurity itself also occupied a different position. The CISO role was less established, board engagement was inconsistent, regulation was less extensive and security budgets were generally smaller. Much has changed since then. But looking back at the management challenges we were discussing more than a decade ago raises an uncomfortable question: Why are we still discussing so many of them? Technology has advanced enormously. Investment has increased. Regulation has expanded. Cybersecurity has achieved unprecedented executive and board visibility. Yet organisations still struggle with governance, accountability, organisational silos, short-termism and execution. Those were management problems in 2015. They remain management problems today. The ‘what’ was never the hardest part One of the central observations behind my early work was that the what of cybersecurity was already reasonably well understood. Standards, control frameworks and good practices had existed for years. Organisations could identify weaknesses, define controls and produce remediation plans. They knew what good cybersecurity looked like. The difficult questions were always the how and the who. How do you implement those controls across complex organisations with conflicting priorities? How do you sustain transformation over several years? Who owns the changes? Who has the authority to make them happen? And who remains accountable when progress stalls? Those questions cannot be answered by a security framework or product. They are governance, management and leadership questions. More than a decade later, that distinction matters even more. Cybersecurity has progressed — but management has lagged There is no question that cybersecurity capabilities have improved. Detection and response have matured. Cloud security has developed rapidly. Identity management has become a central protection discipline. Security operations are increasingly automated, and AI is transforming both attack and defence. Large organisations now operate substantial security functions supported by extensive technology portfolios, specialist providers and advisers. But increased sophistication has not eliminated fundamental management weaknesses. CISOs can remain accountable for issues they lack the authority to resolve. Technology and security strategies can develop on separate tracks. Business executives can still treat cybersecurity as a service delivered by the CISO rather than a dimension of the processes, applications and activities they own themselves. Governance can produce extensive reporting without effective decision-making. Transformation programmes can identify the right problems without necessarily resolving them. The language has evolved. The underlying management dynamics often have not. The CISO reporting-line debate misses the point The persistent debate around where the CISO should report illustrates the problem. For decades, organisations have debated whether the CISO should report to the CIO, CEO, COO, CRO or another senior executive. The CIO reporting line has attracted particular criticism because of a perceived conflict between technology delivery and cybersecurity protection. But if decades of discussion have failed to produce a universally satisfactory answer, perhaps the real problem lies elsewhere. Maybe the more fundamental question is: What does the organisation expect the CISO to be? Some organisations see the CISO primarily as a technology security leader. Others position the role as an independent control function. Some expect the CISO to coordinate resilience, while others increasingly view the position as a strategic business protection role. Those are very different jobs. Until organisations clarify the purpose, authority and accountability of the CISO, debates about reporting lines will continue because organisational structure is being asked to compensate for ambiguity around the role itself. Moving the CISO around the organisation chart cannot resolve that ambiguity. CIO-CISO tension is not necessarily conflict The supposed conflict between CIO and CISO needs a proper reality check. The two executives inevitably face different pressures. CIOs balance cost, delivery, availability, innovation and transformation. CISOs must challenge weaknesses and ensure protection and resilience remain adequate. That creates tension. But tension can be constructive and does not have to become conflict. Nor does moving the CISO outside the CIO organisation eliminate those competing priorities. Any modern CIO should acknowledge that cybersecurity is inseparable from architecture, cloud, identity, DevOps, digital transformation, AI and resilience. CIOs and CISOs must collaborate regardless of the formal reporting structure. What organisations really need is a governance model capable of resolving disagreements when legitimate priorities compete. That is a leadership and management requirement, not something structural separation can solve on its own. Cybersecurity may be undermanaged, not just underfunded Security spending tells a similar story. Cybersecurity investment has risen substantially over the past decade, and some organisations undoubtedly still require more resources. But persistent weaknesses after years of increasing expenditure should lead executives to ask whether funding is always the central issue. Money can buy technology, people and expertise. It can finance transformation and accelerate remediation. What it cannot automatically do is establish strategic priorities, create clear accountability, resolve organisational politics, force collaboration or ensure transformation programmes achieve their objectives. Again, those outcomes depend on leadership and management. Cybersecurity can be underfunded, but quite often it is also undermanaged . The distinction matters because it changes the executive conversation from “How much more do we need to spend?” to “Are we converting the investment we already make into sustainable capability?” Compliance is necessary, but it cannot substitute for management The expansion of regulation and certification schemes has created genuine benefits. It can establish minimum standards, impose accountability and force cybersecurity onto executive agendas. But compliance has inherent limitations. An organisation can satisfy formal requirements while carrying substantial structural weaknesses. An audit finding can be closed without addressing the management problem behind it. Certification can demonstrate that processes exist without proving that an organisation will behave effectively during a serious incident. When showing activity becomes more important than building sustainable capabilities, compliance runs the risk of providing reassurance without necessarily delivering protection. Board awareness was only the first step Over the past decade, cybersecurity has also achieved something the industry demanded for years: It has reached the boardroom. That matters, but board visibility does not automatically produce effective governance. Many organizations are totally technology-dependent and their boards already understand the importance of cyber protection and resilience The old argument that CISOs need to convince boards of the importance of cybersecurity and the need to invest in it, is increasingly outdated. The more important issue is what boards do next. Boards should challenge whether strategic priorities are clear, whether executive accountability is effective, whether transformation is progressing and whether investment is creating sustainable capability. They also need to understand whether assumptions about resilience have been tested. Board awareness was necessary. Board responsibility is the more important issue now. Breaking the cybersecurity spiral of failure These management weaknesses help explain why cybersecurity transformation repeatedly loses momentum. A serious incident creates urgency. Urgency releases funding. Remediation accelerates and visible progress is made. Eventually, the pressure declines. Executive attention moves elsewhere. Longer-term structural problems become harder to prioritise. Transformation slows down. Then another incident restarts the process. I have described this as the Cybersecurity Spiral of Failure . Organisations can spend substantial amounts during every cycle and make genuine technical improvements while leaving intact the management conditions that created the weaknesses in the first place. Poor accountability remains. Governance struggles with difficult decisions. Priorities change. Corporate or geographical silos inhibit execution. Short-term pressures displace long-term transformation. Breaking that cycle requires management discipline and strategic continuity — not simply another security programme. Cybersecurity cannot remain the CISO’s problem Perhaps the most important lesson is that cybersecurity cannot become sustainable while organisations continue treating it primarily as the CISO’s responsibility. The CISO has an essential role in providing expertise, strategic direction, coordination and challenge. But the organisation must execute. The CIO needs to ensure technology architectures and services are secure and resilient. Business executives need to accept accountability for the processes and applications they own. Corporate functions must discharge the security responsibilities attached to their authority. Executive management must resolve competing priorities. The board must provide oversight and strategic continuity. The CISO cannot substitute for those responsibilities. The principle should be straightforward: Accountability must follow authority. The objective is not to turn every executive into a cybersecurity specialist. It is to make cybersecurity part of normal management. The technology will change. The management principles won’t There will always be another technology wave. AI will continue to transform business practices. Quantum computing may force major cryptographic transformation. Cloud architectures will continue evolving. Digital ecosystems will become even more interconnected. The security industry will respond with new products, frameworks and methodologies. But organisations need management principles capable of surviving those technology cycles: Clear priorities. Accountability aligned with authority. Governance capable of turning disagreement into decisions. Strong CIO-CISO collaboration. Genuine business ownership. Sustained board oversight. And disciplined execution. That brings us back to the question we started with: Why do cybersecurity observations from 2015 still sound so contemporary? Because many of the hardest cybersecurity problems were never primarily technological. They concern leadership, accountability, governance, organisational politics, short-termism and execution. They cannot be patched, outsourced or solved simply by moving the CISO to another reporting line. They have to be managed. Cybersecurity has become a core business protection capability. It is fundamentally a management challenge supported by technology — not a technology challenge that management somehow needs to accommodate.
summary: When I started writing regularly about cybersecurity management in 2015 , the environment looked very different. Cloud computing was still reshaping enterprise technology. Ransomware had not become the industrialised threat it is today. Artificial intelligence was not driving boardroom discussions.

title: AI agents aren’t ‘going rogue.’ Frontier labs are skipping security basics.
raw_text: Since July, US frontier AI labs and other AI leaders have revealed a string of incidents in which their models accessed external computer systems without authorization, events popularly described as AI agents “going rogue.” The most well-known and studied of these incidents is OpenAI’s hack into Hugging Face, which OpenAI initially characterized as “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities,” and later said was due to “misaligned behavior,” or behavior its creators did not intend. Following news of the Hugging Face incident, Anthropic revealed that one of its models gained unauthorized access to the production infrastructure of three organizations; Meta said one of its AI models hacked another company ​during cybersecurity testing; and Google confessed that its Gemini model carried out three “undirected computer hacks.” Although press reports and the model providers themselves use language such as rogue agents or misalignment, cybersecurity experts who spoke with CSO argue that language obscures a simple truth: These incidents were caused by inexcusable failures by the frontier labs to implement cybersecurity practices that have been well-known for decades. [ See also: Securing AI agents: Key controls and best practices and Who is accountable when your AI agent goes rogue? ] Compounding the problem, according to a half dozen cybersecurity experts CSO interviewed at three industry conferences in September and in subsequent conversations, is that the frontier labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, have rejected their advice on how to improve their cybersecurity risk management practices to avoid these kinds of surreptitious hacks, often lumping cybersecurity practices under “AI safety,” in which they believe they have superior expertise. “They are not as good as they think they are, honestly,” Gary McGraw, co-founder of the Berryville Institute of Machine Learning, tells CSO. “It would be better if they had more respect for expertise that is hard-earned from people in all sorts of subsets of security, like forensics or security engineering, building sandboxes, setting up or monitoring network security situations.” Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI responded to CSO’s requests for comment. Inexcusable failures on cybersecurity basics, particularly containment According to the cybersecurity professionals CSO spoke with, one of the biggest cybersecurity failures by the frontier AI labs is the lack of implementation of tried-and-true containment practices that stretch back to the 1990s, such as setting up secure sandboxes that would effectively bar agents from escaping their test environments. “These are things that we’ve been dealing with for years,” Rob T. Lee, chief AI officer and chief of research at SANS Institute, tells CSO. “There’s no reason why every single time this happens, it’s, ‘Oops, we don’t know how they got out.’” “You can tell that their security teams are fairly nascent,” Lee says. “Folks on the cybersecurity containment side do argue that the majority of reasons that we’re seeing containment breached is that it’s not set up correctly.” Lee adds, “The Hugging Face incident definitively showed that it wasn’t the fact that the agents were super smart. It’s that there literally was a hole that was exploited because it was not configured correctly on the containment side.” Dan Wallach, expert technical resident at RAND’s Center on AI, Security, and Technology, thinks the security failures of the AI labs boil down to the fact that they don’t prioritize cybersecurity. “I would say they are not prioritizing cybersecurity,” he tells CSO. “I don’t think I can say that for all of the labs,” Wallach says, pointing to French AI lab Mistral’s launch of its Large 4 AI model, which the company said tried to operate beyond its testing environment before Mistral cut it off. And, he adds, “It’s not rocket science to isolate one of these AI things. Security people have been talking about how to do either air-gapping, so there’s literally no electrical way for data to get from here to here, or absent that, to have really strong egress control to make sure that nothing pushes through.” On top of that, the frontier labs appear to be conducting insufficient monitoring of their agents’ behavior. The Hugging Face incident “went on for days, and nobody noticed,” Wallach says. “People started these experiments and weren’t watching them. That’s an absence of control. And then they’re surprised by what happened.” Divorcing safety from security One barrier to persuading frontier labs to up their security game is the intense focus they have on what they call “safety,” which they don’t extend to traditional cybersecurity practices. “I can see how security behavior looks like AI safety,” RAND’s Wallach says. “But if the way that you’re evaluating this AI tool is by unleashing it on the internet and seeing what happens, then this is what classical security tooling is for.” SANS Institute’s Lee says, “If these frontier labs really wanted to test their stuff, they need to beef up their cybersecurity component. But their gut reaction in the response to their agents getting out is to say, ‘It’s not a cybersecurity problem.’ It has literally become an AI safety problem, which is divorced from the cybersecurity side.” Many AI experts suggest that if the AI companies were to embrace advice from cybersecurity specialists, it could help put an end to the kind of unrestrained AI agent behavior causing concerns. “AI safety focuses on the rules of the road,” Lee says. “Everything is about guardrail rules.” But “I do believe cybersecurity can contain AI,” he says. “We just need to be in the room where it happens and have a seat at the table. It’s important for our field to be as close to the AI safety folks as possible.” Bad cybersecurity could increase liability If frontier labs are overlooking cybersecurity fundamentals that could reduce or eliminate the types of incidents that have created widespread concerns, that strengthens the case that they should be held liable for their “rogue” agents. The insurance industry is already lining up on the side of holding AI industry executives liable for these actions. Democratic Senators have introduced legislation that would hold AI agent operators liable for hacking incidents. Even the AI-friendly White House has seemingly concluded that the companies should be held liable for their errant agents, while the US Federal Trade Commission is conducting a probe into Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI labs into the dangers their technologies pose to consumers. However, in recent legislative and council hearings, lab representatives have held fast to the notion that they are not responsible for AI agents run amok. Experts say this position is untenable, particularly in light of the labs’ cybersecurity failures. BIML’s McGraw characterizes the labs’ position as: “Don’t send the lawyers to us, send it to our program. It’s our program’s fault.” His assessment of that argument: “That’s just high BS.” He also questions whether the labs’ operational failures undermine confidence in their broader security capabilities. “They live inside their own bubble,” he says. “The fact that they cannot do clear, easy operations properly does not bode well for their capabilities in security engineering, which is much harder to do.” SANS Lee says, “That’s where the traceability for both liability and insurance comes into play, because if one of these agents is detected, and they’re able to trace it back to the person that initiated it, liability’s going to kick in and say, ‘Hey, you, you broke the law, ergo, we need to prosecute.’” What security leaders should do now Even as evidence mounts that frontier labs are not implementing sound cybersecurity practices, and the debate over liability remains unsolved , CISOs and other security leaders can take steps to protect themselves from AI model misfires. First, when it comes to assessing tools based on frontier lab models, “I would always get an external entity to help with that,” McGraw says. “AI is extremely powerful and extremely useful, but it comes with very serious grown-up risks that do impact the enterprise. Identify those risks, put in the right controls, make sure that AI adoption is not just arbitrary and willy-nilly and all over the enterprise, but has some centralized authority that is looking at the problem, and then get ready for the next big thing, which is swarms of agents.” For Lee, the best protection is to ask the right questions. “It starts with asking the right questions and then finding the tools and capabilities for those [AI labs] that are able to demonstrate a higher level of cybersecurity competency,” he says. “You’re really looking for the people on the teams that are dealing with really hard problems.” But fundamentally, the best preparation to deal with AI model cyber weaknesses is to make sure all the long-standing cybersecurity risk management practices are in place across the organization. “This is the least exciting part of the discussion,” Wallach says. “It’s the cyber version of ‘eat your vegetables.’” “We need to re-engineer our software so it has better security,” he adds. “We need to have multi-factor authentication on all of our accounts. We need to eat our vegetables from a defensive cyber perspective. And we know how to do it.” See also: Securing AI agents: Key controls and best practices Who is accountable when your AI agent goes rogue?
